name: Software Supply-Chain Security
description: Security of dependencies, package registries, build systems, CI/CD, and code provenance.

uss.narrative:
The earliest work in this set framed software supply-chain security as an ecosystem-trust problem. "Small World with High Risks: A Study of Security Threats in the npm Ecosystem" (USENIX 2019) mapped how a handful of maintainers and deeply nested transitive dependencies create outsized risk across npm, making the case that a single compromised package can ripple through thousands of downstream projects. In parallel, "in-toto: Providing farm-to-table guarantees for bits and bytes" (USENIX 2019) attacked the problem from the provenance side, proposing a cryptographic framework to attest that every step of the build pipeline was carried out by the right actor in the right order. Together these two set the field's twin agendas: measuring real-world ecosystem risk, and building verifiable trust into the supply chain.

The early 2020s broadened the threat surface from packages to the whole reuse-and-build stack. A cluster of work tackled vulnerability propagation through reused code: "V0Finder: Discovering the Correct Origin of Publicly Reported Software Vulnerabilities" (USENIX 2021) traced where bugs actually originated, while "MOVERY" (USENIX 2022) and later "V1SCAN" (USENIX 2023) pushed precise detection of modified, cloned vulnerable components in C/C++. At the same time attention turned to CI/CD itself as an attack surface: "Characterizing the Security of Github CI Workflows" (USENIX 2022) and "ARGUS: A Framework for Staged Static Taint Analysis of GitHub Workflows and Actions" (USENIX 2023) showed that automated build and deploy pipelines were under-examined and exploitable. Registry-level deception also became a named research target with "Exploring the Unchartered Space of Container Registry Typosquatting" (USENIX 2022) and "Beyond Typosquatting: An In-depth Look at Package Confusion" (USENIX 2023), which systematized how developers get tricked into pulling the wrong artifact.

The most recent shift, from 2024 onward, is the entanglement of machine learning with the supply chain, in both directions. As offense, "An LLM-Assisted Easy-to-Trigger Backdoor Attack on Code Completion Models" (USENIX 2024), building on the earlier "You Autocomplete Me: Poisoning Vulnerabilities in Neural Code Completion" (USENIX 2021), showed that AI coding assistants are themselves a poisonable link in the chain. As defense, "DONAPI" (USENIX 2024) and "MalGuard" (USENIX 2025) apply behavior- and ML-based detection to catch malicious npm and PyPI packages at scale. The frontier work, "ChainFuzz: Exploiting Upstream Vulnerabilities in Open-Source Supply Chains" (USENIX 2025), closes a loop the field opened in 2019: rather than just measuring or detecting risk, it actively reasons about how upstream bugs become exploitable downstream. The trajectory runs from "this ecosystem is fragile" to fine-grained provenance, build-pipeline and registry hardening, and now AI-era attack and defense.

ndss.narrative:
The earliest work in this collection framed supply-chain risk as a problem of untrusted code running inside your own application. BreakApp (NDSS 2018) started from the observation that large systems pull in many third-party modules and argued for automatically compartmentalizing them, so a compromised dependency could not take over the whole process. Soon after, the focus widened from the running application to the developer ecosystem around it: How Bad Can It Git? (NDSS 2019) showed that public GitHub repositories were bleeding secrets at scale, while Automating Patching of Vulnerable Open-Source Software Versions in Application Binaries (NDSS 2019) tackled the flip side — the vulnerable OSS that developers had already shipped into binaries and mobile apps.

The threat model sharpened around the package registry itself. Towards Measuring Supply Chain Attacks on Package Managers for Interpreted Languages (NDSS 2021) named and measured the now-canonical attack — malicious or typosquatted packages pushed through npm and PyPI-style registries — and set the agenda for much of what followed. Adjacent work stretched the same provenance concerns into other domains: FANDEMIC (NDSS 2022) into firmware and IoT power-management chips, and BlockScope (NDSS 2023) into vulnerabilities silently propagated across forked blockchain projects. UntrustIDE (NDSS 2024) then pushed the attack surface all the way onto the developer's desk, exploiting weaknesses in VS Code extensions.

By 2025 the field had matured into two parallel efforts: better detection inside ecosystems, and the machinery of trust and provenance. On the detection side, NodeMedic-FINE and Enhancing Security in Third-Party Library Reuse (both NDSS 2025) automated finding and exploiting known vulnerabilities, VeriBin (NDSS 2025) verified vendor patches at the binary level, and Welcome to Jurassic Park (NDSS 2025) audited the newer Deno ecosystem built to fix npm's failings. On the trust side, JBomAudit (NDSS 2025) stress-tested SBOMs as a compliance remedy, Rethinking Trust in Forge-Based Git Security (NDSS 2025) questioned what Git forges actually guarantee, and Attributing Open-Source Contributions is Critical but Difficult (NDSS 2025) showed that even knowing who wrote critical code remains hard.

The most recent work at NDSS 2026 splits between precision tooling and the softer edges of the ecosystem. Bullseye detects prototype pollution in npm packages with working exploits, From Noise to Signal precisely maps which npm packages a known vulnerability actually affects, and VulSCA and RTrace bring accurate composition analysis and runtime visibility to the messier world of C/C++ shared libraries. Alongside these, two studies point at the human and trust layer: Action Required (NDSS 2026) is a mixed-methods look at insecure practices in GitHub Actions CI/CD pipelines, and Understanding the Status and Strategies of the Code Signing Abuse Ecosystem (NDSS 2026) documents, for the first time, real-world malware abusing the code-signing certificates that the whole provenance story ultimately rests on. The arc runs from isolating a bad module inside one app to securing the entire pipeline — registries, forges, build systems, and signing authorities — that software now flows through.

sp.narrative:
The earliest work in this list treats supply-chain security as a patch-and-hardware hygiene problem. SPIDER (S&P 2020) tackled the reality that a fix landing in one open-source repository often fails to propagate to the many forks and downstream projects that share its code, leaving known-vulnerable copies in the wild. ICAS (S&P 2020) came at provenance from the silicon end, estimating how susceptible an IC layout is to additive hardware Trojans. Together they framed the two questions the field would keep returning to: does a fix actually reach everyone who needs it, and can you trust an artifact you didn't build yourself?

The 2022-2023 window is where the field matured into a distinct research area, pushed heavily by the fallout from SolarWinds. Committed to Trust (S&P 2022) and the qualitative "Always Contribute Back" study (S&P 2023) turned to the humans and trust relationships behind open-source projects, while the widely cited SoK: Taxonomy of Attacks on Open-Source Software Supply Chains (S&P 2023) gave everyone a shared vocabulary for the attack surface. The rest of that cohort filled in the concrete threat classes: package-registry abuse (Investigating Package Related Security Threats in Software Registries, S&P 2023), the promise and pain of reproducible builds (the "It's like flossing your teeth" paper, S&P 2023), CI pipelines as an attack surface (Continuous Intrusion, S&P 2023), and better security-patch detection with GraphSPD (S&P 2023). BadEncoder (S&P 2022) quietly opened a second front by showing that a poisoned pre-trained encoder is itself a compromised dependency.

By 2024-2025 the "dependency" being attacked was increasingly a model or a dataset rather than a source package. Poisoning Web-Scale Training Datasets is Practical (S&P 2024) showed real, low-cost poisoning of the data crawls that models are built from, and TrojanPuzzle (S&P 2024) plus Poisoned ChatGPT Finds Work for Idle Hands (S&P 2024) demonstrated that poisoned code-suggestion models push insecure code into developers' hands. Alongside this AI turn, the classical registry-and-provenance line kept advancing with measurement and defense work: Signing in Four Public Software Package Registries (S&P 2024), Hey, Your Secrets Leaked! (S&P 2025) on credential leakage, and My Model is Malware to You (S&P 2025), which weaponized TensorFlow APIs to smuggle malware inside a model file.

The most recent papers show the frontier splitting cleanly. On the classical infrastructure side, COSSETER (S&P 2026) uses demand-driven static analysis to shrink over-broad GitHub Actions permissions, and Death Is Not the End (S&P 2026) tracks how automatic updates change vulnerability lifespans in container ecosystems. On the AI side, the machine-learning artifact is now treated as a first-class supply-chain component under active attack: Your Compiler is Backdooring Your Model (S&P 2026) finds backdoors introduced by deep-learning compilers, On the (In)Security of Loading Machine Learning Models (S&P 2026) targets the deserialization step itself, and Exploiting Leaderboards for Large-Scale Distribution of Malicious Models (S&P 2026) shows model hubs as a distribution channel. Parasites in the Toolchain (S&P 2026) extends the same registry-abuse playbook to the emerging MCP tool ecosystem, signaling that every new distribution channel inherits the old supply-chain problems.

ccs.narrative:
Software supply-chain security at CCS emerged as a distinct area tracking the growing threat of malicious packages, compromised dependencies, and insufficient code signing. Model-Reuse Attacks on Deep Learning Systems (CCS 2018) foreshadowed the supply-chain concern in ML: sharing pre-trained models enables attackers to compromise downstream users without touching their code. A Qualitative Study of Dependency Management and Its Security Implications (CCS 2020) explained the human factors causing developers to leave vulnerable dependencies unpatched, despite tooling availability.

The community built detection and prevention tools through 2020-2021. Towards Using Source Code Repositories to Identify Software Supply Chain Attacks (CCS 2020) identified malicious code injection by detecting repository inconsistencies. Locating the Security Patches for Disclosed OSS Vulnerabilities with Vulnerability-Commit Correlation Ranking (CCS 2021) automated patch localization for CVEs. Preventing Dynamic Library Compromise on Node.js via RWX-Based Privilege Reduction (CCS 2021) reduced the blast radius of compromised npm packages by restricting their permissions.

Code signing infrastructure matured in 2022-2023. Sigstore: Software Signing for Everybody (CCS 2022) introduced a free, keyless signing system for software artifacts that has since been adopted by major package ecosystems including npm and PyPI. Speranza: Usable, Privacy-friendly Software Signing (CCS 2023) addressed the developer-privacy cost of identity-linked signatures.

milestones.title: Model-Reuse Attacks on Deep Learning Systems
milestones.note: Showed that malicious pre-trained models compromise any downstream system that reuses them, an early ML supply-chain attack.

milestones.title: A Qualitative Study of Dependency Management and Its Security Implications
milestones.note: Explained the developer decision-making patterns that allow vulnerable dependencies to persist in production codebases.

milestones.title: Locating the Security Patches for Disclosed OSS Vulnerabilities with Vulnerability-Commit Correlation Ranking

milestones.note: Reduced compromised npm library impact using RWX-based privilege constraints on third-party library code.

milestones.note: Eliminated supply-chain vulnerabilities by using active learning to regenerate minimal-privilege component replacements.

milestones.note: Introduced a free keyless software signing system adopted by major package ecosystems to authenticate code provenance.

milestones.note: Addressed developer identity privacy in software signing, providing usable signing without exposing contributor identities.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this area treated third-party code as a measurement and isolation problem. NDSS 2018's "BreakApp: Automated, Flexible Application Compartmentalization" asked how to run untrusted modules without granting them the host's full privileges, while CCS 2018's "Model-Reuse Attacks on Deep Learning Systems" was an early hint that reused pre-trained components carry hidden risk. The field's center of gravity arrived a year later with "Small World with High Risks: A Study of Security Threats in the npm Ecosystem" (USENIX 2019), which quantified how sprawling transitive dependency trees concentrate trust in a handful of maintainers, and "How Bad Can It Git?" (NDSS 2019), which showed developers routinely leak secrets into public repositories. Alongside the diagnosis came the first defenses: "in-toto: Providing farm-to-table guarantees for bits and bytes" (USENIX 2019) proposed verifying the entire chain from source to shipped artifact.

The early 2020s turned measurement into infrastructure and process. Qualitative studies such as "A Qualitative Study of Dependency Management and Its Security Implications" (CCS 2020) and "Committed to Trust" (S&P 2022) examined why developers under-invest in updating and vetting dependencies, while "Towards Using Source Code Repositories to Identify Software Supply Chain Attacks" (CCS 2020) and "Characterizing the Security of Github CI Workflows" (USENIX 2022) shifted attention to registries and build pipelines as attack surfaces. The signal breakthrough was "Sigstore: Software Signing for Everybody" (CCS 2022), which made keyless signing and transparency logs deployable at ecosystem scale — provenance ideas from in-toto finally reaching everyday developers. By S&P 2023, "SoK: Taxonomy of Attacks on Open-Source Software Supply Chains" consolidated the fragmented field into a shared vocabulary, and "Beyond Typosquatting: An In-depth Look at Package Confusion" (USENIX 2023) alongside "Investigating Package Related Security Threats in Software Registries" (S&P 2023) mapped the full space of registry-level deception.

A parallel thread grew steadily around tracking known vulnerabilities through reused code — from "SPIDER" (S&P 2020) and "V0Finder" (USENIX 2021) to "GraphSPD" (S&P 2023) and "V1SCAN" (USENIX 2023) — reflecting that much supply-chain risk is inherited, not injected. Then the AI supply chain became a front of its own: "Poisoning Web-Scale Training Datasets is Practical" (S&P 2024) showed the data feeding models is a cheap, attackable pipeline, while "TrojanPuzzle" (S&P 2024) and "An LLM-Assisted Easy-to-Trigger Backdoor Attack on Code Completion Models" (USENIX 2024) demonstrated that the code-suggestion tools developers now trust can be covertly corrupted.

The most recent work, clustered at NDSS and S&P 2026, extends every one of these threads. The CI/CD and registry lines continue with "Action Required: A Mixed-Methods Study of Security Practices in GitHub Actions" (NDSS 2026), "Bullseye" for prototype pollution in npm (NDSS 2026), and "Understanding the Status and Strategies of the Code Signing Abuse Ecosystem" (NDSS 2026), which shows attackers subverting the very signing trust that Sigstore tried to strengthen. Vulnerability-tracking matures with "VulSCA" and "From Noise to Signal" (both NDSS 2026), and "Death Is Not the End" (S&P 2026) follows how vulnerabilities persist across automatic container updates. Most striking is how thoroughly the machine-learning supply chain has arrived as first-class subject matter: "On the (In)Security of Loading Machine Learning Models," "Exploiting Leaderboards for Large-Scale Distribution of Malicious Models," and "Your Compiler is Backdooring Your Model" (all S&P 2026) treat model files, model hubs, and DL compilers as supply-chain artifacts in their own right — closing the loop back to the 2018 warning about reusing pre-trained components, now at full ecosystem scale.
